A point I emphasize again and again is that the relation between income and fertility is changing quickly, both within and between countries.

To make this point between countries, I take the total fertility rate (TFR) of up to 158 countries from the UN World Population Prospects and their GDP per capita from the Maddison Project, measured at purchasing power parity and in constant 2011 prices (that is, the data already correct for differences in price levels across countries and for inflation). I am not a big fan of the UN World Population Prospects, but this way nobody can accuse me of being selective with my sources.

Then I plot TFR against GDP per capita for 1950 (the start of the sample), 1985 (the midpoint of the sample), and 2022 (the last year in Maddison’s dataset).

The left panel includes all countries except the six Gulf oil exporters (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman), whose wealth comes from oil rents, not from their level of economic development. In the right panel, I also remove sub-Saharan Africa, a region with very poor data on TFR and GDP per capita.

Start with 1950 and 1985. Plot the two curves, and you will have trouble telling them apart. Countries with $2,000 of GDP per capita had 6.1 children per woman in 1950 and 5.9 in 1985. Countries with $5,000 had 4.3 in 1950 and 4.6 in 1985. Countries with $10,000 had 2.8 in both years. Countries got richer and had fewer children, but they moved down the same curve. In 1985, as in 1950, fertility dropped fastest between $5,000 and $10,000, and the typical country reached replacement (about 2.1 children per woman) only at around $14,000. Mexico, with $10,000 of GDP per capita, had 4.1 children per woman. Argentina, with $11,000, had 3.1.

And the relationship between TFR and GDP per capita held despite many other changes. For example, child mortality collapsed at every income level, literacy and life expectancy rose, again at every income level, modern contraceptive methods spread widely, and international organizations and local governments sponsored aggressive family-planning programs across Asia and Latin America from the 1960s. Nothing seemed to matter.

After 1985, the slope of the curve became much smaller (in absolute value) as the left end of the curve started falling quite fast while the right end of the curve barely changed. Interestingly, most of the fall came between 1985 and 1995, well before cell phones and social media (everyone’s favorite explanation) reached anyone outside a small elite of wealthy and highly educated persons.

At $2,000 of GDP per capita, fertility went from 5.9 children per woman in 1985 to 4.0 in 2022, a drop of 1.9 children. But at $20,000 of GDP per capita, fertility was 1.7 children per woman in 1985 and the same 1.7 in 2022.

Similarly, countries with 2.1 children per woman (roughly the replacement rate) were at $14,000 in 1985 but at $11,700 in 2022

Take Sri Lanka. Sri Lanka’s GDP per capita is $11,200, roughly the income at which the 2022 curve crosses replacement. According to the UN World Population Prospects, Sri Lanka has 2.0 children per woman in 2022, while the United States, with five times Sri Lanka’s income, has 1.7. The United States last had Sri Lanka’s income in 1923, when American women had about three children. And according to the most recent data from their national statistical agencies, Sri Lanka is in 2025 at 1.37 children per woman and the United States at 1.57. Sri Lanka has undershot American fertility by a considerable margin (yes, 1.37 is much lower than 1.57) a century before reaching American income.

I also decomposed the change in average TFR across countries into two parts. The first is the change from countries getting richer while moving along a fixed curve. The second is the change from the curve itself shifting, holding each country’s income fixed. 

From 1950 to 1985, almost all of the fall in TFR comes from countries getting richer. Remember: the curve barely moved. 

From 1985 to 2022, about 40% comes from countries getting richer and about 60% from the curve shifting down. That is the big surprise.

Is sub-Saharan Africa driving this result? Yes and no. In the right panel, we can see that the 1950 and 1985 curves barely change when we drop sub-Saharan Africa. Interestingly, the 2022 curve becomes almost flat. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, 92 of the 108 countries with more than $2,500 of GDP per capita have a TFR below 2.5. Most of the income gradient left in 2022 is an African gradient.

Why did the relation between TFR and GDP per capita hold for 35 years (in fact, for at least the early 1800s) and then fall? I do not have a proof, but my conjecture is that low fertility is driven not by income itself but by “modernity.” As I have explained in many posts, by “modernity” I mean the combination of phenomena such as large bureaucratic organizations, mass education, credentials, formal labor markets, and mass media. Until the 1980s, these features of modern life arrived together with economic development and high income. After 1990, the “modernity package” began to reach countries well ahead of income: secondary schooling for girls, television, and integration into global supply chains. Income stopped being a good proxy for “modernity,” so the curve drawn against income fell.

We are only beginning to glimpse the future of “modernity” without economic development. Mexico or Sri Lanka now have the fertility of Japan or Germany, but without the incomes of rich countries, without their state capability, and without their capacity to attract immigration. Becoming rich is no longer a precondition for having few children. Instead, for most of the planet, getting old before getting rich is the new normal.

By 1900, the regional differences got more pronounced and peaked in 1930. There was a strong urban/rural difference, but the Protestant/Catholic divide can clearly be seen as well, especially in French-speaking Switzerland, where Catholic Fribourg and Valais had more than double the TFR of the westernmost Protestant cantons.
The Baby Boom of the 1960s lifted the TFRs across the country, but the previous pattern remained mostly in place. In conservative and Catholic-majority central Switzerland, the TFR approached the levels of the American Baby Boom.
By 1990, the pattern changed somewhat to an urban/rural liberal/conservative divide. Appenzell-Innerrhoden, the last entity in the Western world to grant women's suffrage at the end of 1990, maintained the TFR levels of the Baby Boom until that year.
Nowadays, the TFR is low across Switzerland and regional differences have somewhat lost their importance.

What is Traumatic Brain Injury? ​

​Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a physical injury to the brain resulting from a variety of causes including vehicle crashes, falls, sports related injuries, military combat, and assaults. 

As a result, the severity of the injury can fluctuate in degree from mild to severe, sometimes resulting in death. 

While TBI mostly prompts physical damage to the brain, it is also associated with an array of psychological and hrmonal problems. 

These include cognitive disabilities, sleep pattern problems, lack of attention, dizziness, confusion, etc. 

Current Diagnosis of TBI

TBI is currently diagnosed with a subjective physical examination, psychological screen & the typical Glascow test. The patient's injury is usually confirmed with a CT scan. 

CT scans are effective in depicting bleeding around the brain as well as swelling, but limited in their ability to diagnose mild TBI, especially concussions. 

MRIs are more powerful in their imaging ability in comparison to CT scans. But like CT scans, they are unable to detect injury to nerve fibers inside the brain. 

Hence, axonal damage remains undetectable in most occasions. Other radiological exams like positron emission tomography scans are developed for mild TBI but with extremely high cost. 

The most successful first response test is the imPACT test, which is computerized version of the physical and psychological tests. It allows health care personnel to diagnose TBI at the scene of injury by using an integrated electronic applications, but not reliable.
